text: "What Tsvyatko told," the shy Ilcho spoke up, "is a later matter, but I know that Bay Ganyo had come to Prague earlier, stayed for a long time, and sold quite a bit of rose oil. Do you want me to tell you?"
— Since it’s about Bay Ganyo, don’t ask, tell us! — we answered.

— Good. Listen then. Bay Ganyo arrives from Vienna in Prague. He gets off at the station, shoulders his saddlebags, and goes out into the street. The cabmen rush to offer him their services — he makes a sign with his head that he doesn't want them. They take his sign as affirmative, and a carriage pulls up in front of him. Bay Ganyo gets angry, glares, and makes angry gestures. The policeman notices this and orders the carriages to withdraw. Bay Ganyo wonders from whom to find out where Jireček, our historiographer, lives. Jireček lived in Bulgaria, he loves Bulgarians, Bay Ganyo will go to him: "Good day" — "God give you good" — and he might invite him into his house; why should he spend his little money on hotels? — While he is thinking this, a porter with a red cap appears before him and offers to carry his saddlebags. Bay Ganyo asks him if he knows where Jireček lives; the porter answers in the negative, but gives hope that he can be found, and again reaches out his hands to take the saddlebags. Bay Ganyo does not give them to him, for one, because the vials are inside and he might "dash off somewhere," and for another, he sees him well-dressed, who knows how much he will fleece him.

— Your Honor, go ahead, I’ll follow you — says Bay Ganyo politely. — Leave the saddlebags, I will carry them. Bay Ganyo puts forth this politeness with calculation: it will both win the porter over to him and show him that he is not some big and rich man, so that t h a t  o n e doesn’t think of fleecing him.

They walk along, asking at the crossroads where Jireček lives; at last someone realized that the question was about Professor Jireček, told them where to inquire, they inquired and found him. Bay Ganyo says to the porter a "bless you, we thank you" and enters Jireček's lodgings.

— Oh! Good day, Bay Irechek, how are you, are you well? — exclaims Bay Ganyo in a most friendly tone as he enters the host's study. The latter wonderingly offers him his hand, invites him to sit down, and is angry with his memory, which does not remind him who this polite friend is.

— Don't you recognize me? — Bai Ganyo reminded him, mixing "you" (formal) and "you" (informal). — Weren't you a minister in Sofia? — Yes. — Well, I'm from there too! — Bai Ganyo concluded solemnly. — As they say, we are compatriots, heh, heh, heh, of course! Do you remember the article in the "Slavyanin" newspaper?
— Yes, yes, I remember — Jireček replies with restrained condescension.

— Oh, how they had smeared you!... But you just enjoy yourself, don't you care one bit! How much I have praised you!... They say Jireček is this, Jireček is that. — "Forgive me," I say, "it's not so."

Jireček knows the Bulgarians well and is therefore not at all surprised by this familiarity of Bay Ganyo. The conversation continues for several minutes in this tone, then moves to more practical ground: Bay Ganyo praises the host's apartment, hinting to him quite tangibly that "after all, there is room for even one more stranger to be put up here," speaks to him of the hospitality of the Bulgarians, expressing regret that "you see, others are not like us Bulgarians; should a foreigner enter a Bulgarian house, they will feed him, give him drink, and make his bed."

Jireček tries to impress upon him that the apartment is too cramped for his own family. Bay Ganyo turns a deaf ear and expands on the theme of Bulgarian hospitality. From this topic, the conversation turns toward Bay Ganyo’s little business. He informs the host that he has brought rose oil for sale and declares to him: “Tomorrow, if you like, take me to all the factories, I’m willing; you’ll translate for me, since I don’t know the language, eh?”

Jireček hastens to reply that he is not acquainted with the manufacturers of essential oils, as his pursuits are of an entirely different nature, and furthermore, he has no free time; but he will tell him where the Bulgarian students gather, so that someone among them might be of service to him.

"— If you like, so to speak," added Bay Ganyo, "I won't force you. I'll give the lady (is she here?) a vial of oil as well. I know her too, of course (Jireček cannot stop wondering which lady is being referred to). And if you have relatives or friends here, tell them I've brought oil—it's no shame! I'll be hanging around you more often, we'll talk about Bulgaria. And if you like, I'm even willing to stay at your place while I'm in Prague. Eh?"
— Excuse me, but...
"— I say, so to speak, if you please," Bay Ganyo explains muddledly, "it would be better for me at the hotel too, but then I thought, oh well, Jireček is one of us..."
— Thank you for your kindness; I would gladly have you stay at my home, but I do not have any spare rooms. Today, however, you are our guest and will have lunch with us.
— Let's have lunch, why not have lunch! — Bay Ganyo agrees. — And your honor, as they say, if not from mine — you have always eaten from a Bulgarian table.

Jireček is busy with some urgent work, which is interrupted by the entrance of Bay Ganyo. The host is sitting on pins and needles and does not know how to delicately and temporarily dispatch his talkative guest. He rings, a servant appears, whom he instructs to inform the household that a guest from Bulgaria has arrived. A little later, his mother enters. Bay Ganyo barely rises from his chair, makes a double motion toward his forehead with his hand, and condescendingly says: “Oh, hello, greetings, let’s shake hands, there we go, the Bulgarian way. How are you? I’m glad.”
The lady welcomed him kindly and, with a whole series of questions, showed a lively interest in the guest's homeland.
— Well, tell the honest truth now — asked Bay Ganyo, — where is it better, in Prague or in Sofia?

The lady is bewildered, she has not been to Sofia, and at this question Bay Ganyo looks at Jireček with a devilish smile, as if he wants to instill in him his view on women: "Well, she’s a woman, isn’t she, what is there to talk to her about?..."

— "His Grace will dine at home today," Jireček addresses his mother and then, so that he can continue his work, asks her in German to take Bay Ganyo into another room. The lady suggests to Bay Ganyo that they move into the adjacent room. Bay Ganyo looks piercingly at Jireček, looks at the saddlebags with the vials, calculates with his eyebrows: "They said something in German, who knows! But I don't believe it. After all, he was a minister in our country. Well, even ministers aren't worth much, are they! But for this one, I don't believe it" — and then he rises indecisively and follows the lady's direction toward the adjacent room, but as he reaches the door, he turns back, wanting to read the hosts' intentions on their faces, and notices several silent signs which the household members indeed exchanged at that moment; these signs meant: "Try to keep him occupied with something for a longer time, as I have very urgent work," but Bay Ganyo interpreted it otherwise.
"These things here might get in your way," he states, gesturing with his eyes toward the saddlebags.
— Oh, not at all. Please, don't trouble yourself — Jireček replies.

— But they'll still be in your way, I know it. Let me take them into the other room — and he reaches to take them, but the family members politely resist. — Not that I'm afraid, no, it's just that, I said...

They go into the reception room and the lady closes the door behind her so that the noise cannot be heard in the study. She tries in every way to occupy Bay Ganyo with something curious: she offers him various albums, shows him pictures, places a whole pile of illustrations before him, but Bay Ganyo’s mind is elsewhere entirely and he responds to the lady’s courtesies with feigned indifference:
— I don’t want any, thank you: you look at them. How many such pictures and portraits I have seen! Don’t let my youth fool you!

Bay Ganyo looks impatiently at his huge silver watch and begins a very interesting and timely conversation:
— I am very curious to study Europe. Now, for example, let's say, back home when noon comes—they sit down to lunch. With you, it is arranged differently. When do you have lunch, for example?
— We usually have lunch at 5 o'clock, but today we can have lunch earlier. Excuse me, I will leave you for just a minute — said the lady and went out through the other door.

Bay Ganyo sits alone in the parlor, staring distractedly at the paintings, spitting on the carpet every now and then (not that he is hungry, but who knows!), rubbing it with his boots and listening for the slightest noise in the study. At one point, he hears Jireček get up from his chair, take a few steps, and stop. "What a fool I am, why didn't I move my saddlebags into this room." Bay Ganyo sits as if on pins and needles; finally, he can't contain himself, he gets up, steps quietly across the carpet toward the door of the study, leans his ear to the keyhole and listens; he hears only his own rapid breathing and the pounding of blood in his ears. But even here Bay Ganyo does not calm down; he sees nothing through the keyhole and, pressing the door handle indecisively, he opens it, pokes his head mysteriously into the study, and sees Jireček, crouched near his saddlebags in front of a bookcase.

Bay Ganyo snickers at him:
— Hee, hee, hee, are you working, are you working? Hee, hee, hee! Wait, I thought, let me take a peek. Keep on working, it's nothing, I'll close it again.
Jireček looks at him in amazement, without the reason for this peculiar curiosity even crossing his mind.

Lunch is ready. They pass into the dining room and sit around the table: Jireček’s parents, his sister, Bay Ganyo, and he. Bay Ganyo, before lunch begins, starts to cross himself, while smiling, by which he wants to show the hosts that he is not one of those simple little folk and not that he believes all that much, but still, it’s not bad (we are on good terms with the devil, what’s the harm in burning a little incense for the Lord too — for a rainy day).

— I am a lib'ral, from the lib'ral party — he explains, — but every now and then I cross myself, it’s not a bad thing, we’re only human... What is this, is it soup? Ah, I love soup. Chorba is a Turkish dish. And we eat more soup now. Ah, pardon, excuse me, I’ve stained your bundle... Tsk... tsk... tsk... Confound it!...

Carried away by the desire to present himself as a civilized man, Bay Ganyo failed to take the plate of soup properly when the hostess handed it to him, and spilled quite a bit of it onto the table; and before anyone could stop him, he gathered a portion with his spoon and poured it into his plate. The hostess did not want to allow him to eat that soup, but out of delicacy, he shielded his plate with his hands and did not want them to change it for him.

"I have peppers in my saddlebags," Bay Ganyo announced suddenly. He was burning with desire to crumble one of the small peppers into the soup, which appeared altogether too pale for his stomach, but he was embarrassed to take out the peppers lest they think him a boor, so he wanted first to sound out the hosts.
— Yes? Do you have peppers? — Jireček called out.

— Of course I do, I carry peppers with me; you know, "Bulgaria, dear mother" cannot do without a bit of heat — says Bay Ganyo ironically and, without waiting any longer, jumps up from his chair, rushes into the study, drags over his saddlebags, squats over them with his back to the hosts, and brings two peppers to the table.

— Two are enough for the five of us, they are terribly hot — he declares, as he shakes out half a pepper with the seeds into his plate and politely offers the rest to the hosts: — Here, help yourselves, rub some in, heh, heh, heh, the Bulgarian way! No, no, rub it in, listen to me and you will see what it’s like. Well, you know: you can’t force beauty. Wait for me to rub mine in, so I can show you what is called a soup.

And indeed, Bay Ganyo spiced his soup to such a degree that an unaccustomed person would have been poisoned. And he began to slurp; and how the Bulgarian slurps, he is not joking—if three hundred dogs were fighting, they could not drown him out. Large drops of sweat beaded on his forehead and seemed to strive to pour into his plate. Bay Ganyo would take a slurp from the tip of the spoon, set the spoon down, and push down the spicy liquid with two or three mouthfuls of bread; then he would take the spoon again, slurp some soup, sniff inward, and again two or three mouthfuls of bread.

— Here, pass me another little piece of bread. You eat with no bread at all — Bay Ganyo wonders. — Give the Bulgarian bread; we eat a lot of bread; not to boast, but with such a chorba — pardon, with such a soup — I can eat a whole loaf of bread. I'll bet on it.
They didn't make a bet, but even so, Bay Ganyo polished off quite a bit of bread.
"Where do you get this wine from?" Bai Ganyo inquired, not that he was interested in the answer, but just to find an excuse for another glass.
"We'll buy it," the owner replied, "is it good?"

— Ah! Pure stuff! You're buying it, eh? Hand the bottle over here. My stomach is so on fire from that pepper, like red-hot iron, that if I pour the whole bottle down now, it’ll sizzle inside. Eh, back home, wine is half a lev an oka—once you knock back an oka, you’re in business!... Ah, I burped, forgive me: that’s a bit vulgar, I know, but pardon, it’s only human, you can’t hold it in!...

Lunch at Jireček's turned out to be quite lively, thanks to Bay Ganyo. Coffee was served to them in the reception room. In gratitude for the delicious, and above all, filling lunch, Bay Ganyo wanted to treat his host to a cigarette, but as luck would have it, his tobacco was in his saddlebags. To tell the truth, his cigarette case was in his pocket, but he had to find an excuse to check on his saddlebags; he couldn't just leave his vials of rose oil with strangers—anything can happen in this world.
Bay Ganyo won't even hear of the host's refusal to smoke some of his tobacco: "How so, my dear fellow, is it even possible for a man not to smoke Bulgarian tobacco!"

Bay Ganyo lit up and began to slurp his coffee with relish. Now that's what you call slurping!... To find yourself in such a pleasant mood, to spend whole hours with a companion, to be in a room where no one will hear what you're saying, and even if they do, they won't understand you—under such favorable conditions, to restrain yourself and not start talking about politics, that is beyond Bay Ganyo's strength. He could not restrain himself; he poured out his soul:
— Say, Bay Jireček, tell me, your honor, are you a liberal or a conservative? It seems to me you're a conservative, from what I see. And me, if you ask, I can't understand either one of them, but well, let's not offend them... You know, it's business, it's no joke... And shall I tell you the honest truth... (Is there anyone eavesdropping on us here?) Shall I tell you the honest truth? — They're all scoundrels, both of them!... You listen to me, and don't you worry! Scoundrels, every single one of them!... But what can you do? You don't kick against the prick!... A little trade, little enterprises, I have lawsuits in the courts—it's impossible. If you're not with them, you're finished! And besides, I want to be elected, maybe as a deputy, maybe as a mayor. There's profit in those things. People have piled up money, do you know? Fine, but if you don't tip your hat to them—the devil himself couldn't get you elected! That's how it is! I've been through it all, I've lived and breathed these things, so I understand them...
Jireček hardly doubted that his guest understood "those things."
